Change gravity. Watch the fire change.

Pick a gravity, a cabin air and a fan speed. FLINT, calibrated on NASA's Earth tests and checked against NASA's Moon tests, tells you which of four common spacecraft materials keep burning, and why.

The world and the cabin

The fan adds a breeze on top of the rising-air flow that gravity makes. Space stations run fans; fans off is a first step in a fire response.

Four materials found in crew cabins

Who keeps burning?

The oxygen limit is the least oxygen a material needs to keep spreading a flame. If the cabin has more oxygen than the limit, the material burns. "Blown off" means the flow outruns the chemistry; "starved" means the flow is too weak to feed the flame faster than it loses heat.

The whole picture

Oxygen limit at every gravity

Lines below the dashed cabin-oxygen line burn at that gravity. The steep left side of each curve is where weak flow starves the flame; that is why Nomex and polycarbonate burned less readily on the Moon in NASA's tests, and why FLINT predicts they burn more readily on Mars.

Said plainly

What this lab can and cannot tell you

  • FLINT is checked against NASA's four lunar-gravity results at 8.2 psia with no fan (mean error 1.4 points of oxygen). Every other setting is a model extrapolation, and the badge says so.
  • It covers thin solid materials spreading a flame upward in dry oxygen and nitrogen. It does not cover still air in orbit, thick parts, smouldering or other gases.
  • It is a research tool from an independent student team, not a safety certification, and it has not been reviewed by NASA. Inspect the evidence and the Python engine.
